parole.significato: sloe (the small, bitter, wild fruit of the blackthorn)
parole.testo: From a proposed Hispano-Proto-Celtic *agraniō (“sloe”), from earlier Proto-Celtic *agrinyos. From the same source as Irish airne, Welsh eirin, Spanish arañón, and possibly Basque aran (“plum”).
Probably from Proto-Celtic *arona (“ring” or “wheel”) due to these structures first being built in a cylindrical form from woven wood or vegetation.
Perhaps from Proto-Celtic *wādsketi. Compare Welsh gwasg (“pressure, squeezing”), Middle Irish fáiscid (“to press, squeeze”).

Possibly from a reconstructed *bledino-, a derivation of Proto-Celtic *bledyos (“wolf”). Among the many common names in the languages of Europe for Verbascum thapsus (the common mullein), whose long leaves were historically used to make wicks, are the equivalents of “wolf's tail” or “fox's tail”. From Proto-Celtic *brīgos (“strength”). Cognate with Old Irish bríg (“force, power”), Welsh bri (“honour, esteem”).
From archaic cama, from Proto-Celtic *kambos (“bent”).
Probably ultimately from the same Proto-Celtic root as cantó.

Probably ultimately derived from Proto-Celtic *kantos (“corner, rim (of a chariot wheel)”) via Medieval Latin cant(h)ellus, diminutive of canthus (“rim of a chariot wheel”). Compare Provençal cantel (“part, corner”), Catalan chantel (“part, corner, quarter”).
From en- + terc + -ar, from a pre-Romance source such as Proto-Celtic *terkos (“scarce, meagre”), from Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”), compare Irish tearc (“meagre”).
Of Pre-Roman origin, probably from a Proto-Celtic *gēbros (“frozen, wintry”). Compare French givre.
Perhaps from Proto-Celtic *mask- (“black, stained”).
From Proto-Celtic *ɸrik- (“furrow”). Compare Occitan rèc (whence French arrèc) and Basque erreka.
From Proto-Celtic *sesca (“sedge, rushes”).
From a base Proto-Celtic *saliko-, related to Latin salix. Doublet of sarga.
Probably from Proto-Celtic *tullom, *tullos (“hole”). (Compare Irish toll, Welsh twll, both meaning "hole" and Asturian tollu meaning "quagmire".)

parole.significato: an alder, especially the black alder (Alnus glutinosa)
parole.testo: From Proto-Celtic *wernā.
From Old Catalan seixa, from Proto-Celtic *sasyos.

Deverbal from escombrar, from Vulgar Latin *excomborāre, from Proto-Celtic *comboros, derived from *kom- (“with”) + *bereti (“to bear”), or from Latin scōpa, crossed with the Celtic word or influenced by escombrar (compare Occitan escoba, Aragonese escoba and the Ibero-Romance variants).

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; Probably; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Probably from a substrate language. Maybe related with Proto-Brythonic *gwɨmon, from Proto-Celtic *wimmonā, and this possibly from a non-IE substrate language or from Proto-Indo-European *weyb- (“to wind around”). Cognate with Portuguese gamão, Spanish gamón and Galician gamón.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Proto-Basque *karri (“rock”) (compare Basque harri), or from Proto-Celtic *karr- (“rock”) (compare Welsh craig, Irish creag, Manx creg, Armenian քար (kʻar)).

parole.testo: Inherited from Old Catalan truja, from Late Latin troia, of uncertain origin, but possibly * from Latin (porcum de) Troia (“(hog of) Troy”), after the Trojan horse, * or alternatively of Celtic origin, from a Gaulish root *trogja, from a root meaning “to pull” and thence also “fertile," Proto-Celtic
